title: Retelling History as a Confession
overview: Gathered in mourning, the returned exiles pray through their nation's whole history, praising God's patience, admitting repeated failure, and committing to a written agreement.

parts.label: A day of mourning (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: Two days after the joyful festival of chapter 8 ended, the people fast and wear rough sackcloth and dust, signs of grief and humility, and separate from foreigners, probably tied to the mixed marriages dealt with elsewhere in Ezra and Nehemiah. They spend about three hours hearing God's law read and three more confessing, led by Levites (temple assistants) on raised platforms.

parts.label: Creator and Abraham (vv. 5-8)
parts.note: The prayer opens by praising the LORD as the one God who made and keeps alive everything that exists. It then recalls God choosing Abraham and promising his descendants the land, a promise the prayer says God kept.

parts.label: Rescue and wilderness care (vv. 9-21)
parts.note: It retells the escape from Egypt, the sea crossing, the laws given at Mount Sinai, and food and water in the desert. Even when the people made a calf idol and wanted to go back to slavery, the prayer stresses that God kept guiding and feeding them for forty years.

parts.label: The land and a cycle (vv. 22-31)
parts.note: The prayer celebrates taking the land and openly says the Canaanites were handed over to be treated however the Israelites wished. Then a pattern repeats: comfort leads to rebellion, rebellion to oppression, cries for help to rescue, with warning prophets ignored and even killed.

parts.label: Our hardship now (vv. 32-37)
parts.note: The speakers say God has been fair and their people were in the wrong, from the Assyrian invasions until now. Though home again, they are subjects of the Persian empire, whose kings take their harvests in taxes and can command their bodies and livestock.

parts.label: A written promise (v. 38)
parts.note: In response they draw up a binding written agreement, sealed by their leaders, Levites and priests. Its terms and signers follow in the next chapter.

think: When you look back over your own story or your family's, what patterns keep repeating, and what makes them hard to name out loud?
